This determines the minimum viable dataset size, the per-slice coverage required, and the delta threshold a change must exceed — the three numbers every team implementing this loop needs and none of the sources give.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Agent changes produce metric tradeoffs, not uniform improvements
deep_dives.why: The concrete 0.81→0.98 / 0.89→0.72 inversion is the talk's load-bearing evidence that single-metric gates ship regressions. Turning that anecdote into a gating primitive — a protected-success slice plus cross-metric delta rules — is what converts the story into enforceable policy.

This is the single most consequential architectural claim — it dictates how instrumentation must be structured — and the most weakly evidenced.

project_ideas.name: Judge Drift Sentinel
project_ideas.poc: Hold out a human-labeled subset of task-completion judgments from production traces. Score it with three judge model versions, recompute agreement per version, and replay a set of real change experiments through each judge to see whether the gate verdict changes.

project_ideas.based_on: the next frontier of agent observability is closing the loop at agent speed, where agents read traces directly to self-correct
project_ideas.hypothesis: A coding agent given structured trace access to failing runs detects and correctly patches agent regressions at lower latency and lower recurrence rate than human triage on the same incident queue.
project_ideas.measurement: Time-to-diagnosis, patch correctness against a held-out acceptance suite, and recurrence rate on the next regression run; plus the ratio of agent-proposed patches that pass the gate unmodified.
project_ideas.name: Agent-Triage Benchmark
project_ideas.poc: Build a fixed queue of failing traces from a controlled agent, expose them through a structured query interface (not a dashboard), and run two arms: a coding agent that reads traces and proposes patches, and a human engineer doing the same. Apply both patch sets and rerun the regression suite.

project_ideas.based_on: Establish an automated pipeline from production observability failures to regression test datasets.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Automating promotion of failed production traces into versioned test cases increases regression-suite coverage of real failure distribution faster than manual test authoring, and the resulting suite catches a materially higher share of seeded regressions at equal suite size.
project_ideas.measurement: Seeded-regression detection rate of ratchet-built vs hand-built suites at equal case count, plus case-promotion latency from incident to test and the stale-case fraction over time.
project_ideas.name: Failure-to-Test Ratchet Pipeline
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a small deployed agent, capture failing traces, and auto-promote each into a dataset entry with an attached evaluator expectation. Run the ratchet for a fixed period alongside a manually authored suite of matched size, then seed known regressions into both.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Sofia Jakovcevic
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Agent observability and regression testing loops
  • Purpose: To explain the methodology and tooling required for building robust regression loops in AI agent development using production traces and LLM-as-a-judge evaluators. Sofia Jakovcevic, forward deployed engineer at Arize AI, discusses how to turn agent observability into a regression loop that tests every agent change before it ships in production. She covers why agent regressions are different from traditional software bugs (failing at runtime rather than compile time), how to build a 5-step regression loop using datasets, evaluators, baselines, and CI/CD integration, and how moving from human triage to agentic evaluation closes the loop at agent speed.

Topic Map

Introduction to Agent Observability and Regressions

  • Explanation: Introduction of Arize AI as an observability backend for AI systems and framing the core problem: fixing one part of an AI agent often breaks ten other things without the developer knowing.
  • Key claims:
    • Building AI systems can feel intuitive due to high-level abstractions, but the agent's mind is a black box.
    • Observability shines a light in the black box, helping developers understand, evaluate, and iterate on agents.
    • The biggest challenge is not determining what broke, but ensuring that fixing one thing doesn't break ten other things.
  • Examples:
    • A support agent policy edit adds confirmation steps before taking actions, successfully improving action safety from 0.81 to 0.98, but degrading task completion from 0.89 to 0.72 because sessions are left incomplete.
  • Terminology:
    • Arize
    • Observability
    • Black box
    • Action safety
    • Task completion
  • Why it matters: Demonstrates that improving one metric in isolation can hurt overall performance, highlighting the need for comprehensive evaluation suites.

Why Agent Regressions Are Different

  • Explanation: Contrasting traditional software bugs with agent regressions, highlighting why code diffs alone are insufficient for agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Code changes are local, but behavioral effects are non-local.
    • In traditional software, every path is written down and exact paths are known before runtime.
    • In AI agents, logic only exists at runtime, making traces the new source of truth.
    • The diff tells you what changed, but the trace tells you what it actually did.
  • Examples:
    • A one-line prompt change in system_prompt.md appears simple during code review, but at runtime it fundamentally alters the agent's trajectory, tool calling, and sub-agent interactions.
  • Terminology:
    • Code review
    • Runtime failure
    • Traces
    • Silent failures
    • System prompt markdown
  • Why it matters: Explains why static code review fails for LLM applications and establishes production traces as the authoritative source of truth.

Building the Regression Loop: 5-Step Process

  • Explanation: Detailed breakdown of the 5-step process to build a regression loop: selecting a dataset, adding evaluators, running the baseline experiment, making changes and rerunning, and putting the experiment in CI/CD.
  • Key claims:
    • Step 1: Select a dataset pulled from production traces, including representative workflows, known failures, edge cases, and successful workflows to protect.
    • Step 2: Add evaluators to turn subjective metrics into numeric scores using LLM-as-a-judge or code-based/ML-based evaluators.
    • Step 3: Run baseline experiments by running the agent against the dataset with no changes.
    • Step 4: Make one change (prompt, tool, policy, model) and rerun the experiment against the same dataset.
    • Step 5: Put the experiment in CI/CD so every pull request runs through the evaluation gates automatically before merging.
  • Examples:
    • Using LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate task completion on a scale with labels like complete or incomplete.
    • Setting GitHub Actions YAML to run regression python scripts on every pull request.
  • Terminology:
    • Dataset
    • Evaluator
    • LLM-as-a-judge
    • Code evaluator
    • Baseline experiment
    • CI/CD gate
    • GitHub Actions
  • Why it matters: Provides a concrete, reproducible engineering workflow for testing agent changes before deployment.

Closing the Loop at Agent Speed

  • Explanation: Shifting the paradigm from human-in-the-loop triage to agent-driven self-improvement and debugging.
  • Key claims:
    • Human manual triage (reading dashboards and reviewing PRs) is the ultimate bottleneck.
    • The next frontier of agent observability is closing the loop at agent speed, where agents read traces directly to self-correct.
    • Every failure should become a test, and every test should make your next agent harder to break.
    • The best agents don't just learn from failures; they fix themselves.
  • Examples:
    • Using Arize agent playgrounds, remote agent connections, and agent skills to connect coding agents with observability backends.
  • Terminology:
    • Manual bottleneck
    • Agent speed
    • Self-improvement
    • Agent skills
    • Remote agents
  • Why it matters: Envisions the future of AI engineering where agents autonomously diagnose and fix regressions using observability data.

Key Points

Code changes are local, but behavioral effects are systemic

  • Explanation: A minor one-line edit to a prompt can drastically alter downstream tool calls, planning, and execution paths in non-deterministic ways.
  • Evidence: A single line change in system_prompt.md caused unintended degradation in task completion rates despite improving action safety.
  • Practical implication: Never ship prompt or policy changes based solely on intuition or code diffs; always validate against a production test dataset.

Traces are the new source of truth

  • Explanation: Unlike traditional software where logic is explicitly written in source code, agent behavior only materializes at runtime through stochastic LLM interactions.
  • Evidence: Thousands of possible trajectories exist only in runtime traces, not in static code files.
  • Practical implication: Build test suites directly from production traces rather than synthetic test data alone.

Every failure should become a test

  • Explanation: When an agent fails in production or during evaluation, that exact trace and failure case must be ingested back into the regression test suite.
  • Evidence: Failed production runs become new regression test cases, preventing the same bug from recurring.
  • Practical implication: Establish an automated pipeline from production observability failures to regression test datasets.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The 5-Step Agent Regression Loop

  • How it works: A continuous engineering workflow to test agent changes against production data before deployment.
  • Components:
    • Observe: Trace every agent run in production
    • Evaluate: Score live traces with standardized evaluators
    • Change: Edit prompt, model, tool, skill, or policy
    • Test: Run regression experiments in CI/CD against evaluation gates
    • Improve: Ship what passes and feed new failures back into test datasets
  • When to use: Whenever making modifications to LLM prompts, agent policies, tool definitions, or underlying models in production applications.

Examples & Case Studies

A security engineer added a one-line policy requiring the support agent to confirm before taking any action.

  • Illustrates: Unintended side effects of localized prompt changes on multi-step workflows.
  • Lesson: Action safety improved by 17% (+0.17), but task completion dropped by 17% (-0.17), resulting in a net-zero overall average improvement.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Pull real production traces including normal workflows, known failures, edge cases, and successful workflows into evaluation datasets.
    • Combine code-based evaluators for deterministic checks with LLM-as-a-judge evaluators for semantic metrics.
    • Integrate agent evaluation suites into GitHub Actions or CI/CD pipelines as merge gates.
  • Strategic:
    • Treat production traces as the authoritative source of truth for agent behavior.
    • Shift from human manual triage to automated agent-driven self-correction and testing.
    • Ensure every production failure automatically updates and strengthens the regression test suite.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can agents autonomously propose and test prompt or policy fixes based on trace failures?
    • What is the optimal balance between LLM-as-a-judge evaluation cost and accuracy in CI pipelines?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • The diff tells you what changed, but the trace tells you what it actually did (conceptual)
  • The best agents don't just learn from failures; they fix themselves (visionary)

Notable Quotes

"Your agent fix just broke something else." "The diff tells you what changed. The trace tells you what it did." "The logic only exists at runtime." "Every failure should become a test." "The best agents don't just learn from failures. They fix themselves."

Compressed Summary

  • Agent regressions manifest at runtime rather than compile time.
  • Code diffs fail to capture behavioral changes in LLM agents.
  • A 5-step regression loop leverages production traces, evaluators, baselines, and CI gates.
  • LLM-as-a-judge converts subjective agent metrics into actionable numeric scores.
  • Automating evaluation in CI/CD prevents shipping broken agent changes.
  • Keywords: observability, regression, evaluators, traces, agents, cicd
  • Core insight: Agent observability must evolve from a debugging dashboard for humans into an automated regression loop where production failures continuously strengthen agent test suites.

  - A support agent policy edit adds confirmation steps before taking actions, successfully improving action safety from 0.81 to 0.98, but degrading task completion from 0.89 to 0.72 because sessions are left incomplete.
- **Terminology**:
  - Arize
  - Observability
  - Black box
  - Action safety
  - Task completion
- **Why it matters**: Demonstrates that improving one metric in isolation can hurt overall performance, highlighting the need for comprehensive evaluation suites.
### Why Agent Regressions Are Different
- **Explanation**: Contrasting traditional software bugs with agent regressions, highlighting why code diffs alone are insufficient for agents.
- **Key claims**:
  - Code changes are local, but behavioral effects are non-local.
  - In traditional software, every path is written down and exact paths are known before runtime.
  - In AI agents, logic only exists at runtime, making traces the new source of truth.
  - The diff tells you what changed, but the trace tells you what it actually did.
- **Examples**:
  - A one-line prompt change in system_prompt.md appears simple during code review, but at runtime it fundamentally alters the agent's trajectory, tool calling, and sub-agent interactions.
- **Terminology**:
  - Code review
  - Runtime failure
  - Traces
  - Silent failures
  - System prompt markdown
- **Why it matters**: Explains why static code review fails for LLM applications and establishes production traces as the authoritative source of truth.
### Building the Regression Loop: 5-Step Process
- **Explanation**: Detailed breakdown of the 5-step process to build a regression loop: selecting a dataset, adding evaluators, running the baseline experiment, making changes and rerunning, and putting the experiment in CI/CD.
- **Key claims**:
  - Step 1: Select a dataset pulled from production traces, including representative workflows, known failures, edge cases, and successful workflows to protect.
  - Step 2: Add evaluators to turn subjective metrics into numeric scores using LLM-as-a-judge or code-based/ML-based evaluators.
  - Step 3: Run baseline experiments by running the agent against the dataset with no changes.
  - Step 4: Make one change (prompt, tool, policy, model) and rerun the experiment against the same dataset.
  - Step 5: Put the experiment in CI/CD so every pull request runs through the evaluation gates automatically before merging.
- **Examples**:
  - Using LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate task completion on a scale with labels like complete or incomplete.
  - Setting GitHub Actions YAML to run regression python scripts on every pull request.
- **Terminology**:
  - Dataset
  - Evaluator
  - LLM-as-a-judge
  - Code evaluator
  - Baseline experiment
  - CI/CD gate
  - GitHub Actions
- **Why it matters**: Provides a concrete, reproducible engineering workflow for testing agent changes before deployment.
### Closing the Loop at Agent Speed
- **Explanation**: Shifting the paradigm from human-in-the-loop triage to agent-driven self-improvement and debugging.
- **Key claims**:
  - Human manual triage (reading dashboards and reviewing PRs) is the ultimate bottleneck.
  - The next frontier of agent observability is closing the loop at agent speed, where agents read traces directly to self-correct.
  - Every failure should become a test, and every test should make your next agent harder to break.
  - The best agents don't just learn from failures; they fix themselves.
- **Examples**:
  - Using Arize agent playgrounds, remote agent connections, and agent skills to connect coding agents with observability backends.
- **Terminology**:
  - Manual bottleneck
  - Agent speed
  - Self-improvement
  - Agent skills
  - Remote agents
- **Why it matters**: Envisions the future of AI engineering where agents autonomously diagnose and fix regressions using observability data.
## Key Points
### Code changes are local, but behavioral effects are systemic
- **Explanation**: A minor one-line edit to a prompt can drastically alter downstream tool calls, planning, and execution paths in non-deterministic ways.
- **Evidence**: A single line change in system_prompt.md caused unintended degradation in task completion rates despite improving action safety.
- **Practical implication**: Never ship prompt or policy changes based solely on intuition or code diffs; always validate against a production test dataset.
### Traces are the new source of truth
- **Explanation**: Unlike traditional software where logic is explicitly written in source code, agent behavior only materializes at runtime through stochastic LLM interactions.
- **Evidence**: Thousands of possible trajectories exist only in runtime traces, not in static code files.
- **Practical implication**: Build test suites directly from production traces rather than synthetic test data alone.
### Every failure should become a test
- **Explanation**: When an agent fails in production or during evaluation, that exact trace and failure case must be ingested back into the regression test suite.
- **Evidence**: Failed production runs become new regression test cases, preventing the same bug from recurring.
- **Practical implication**: Establish an automated pipeline from production observability failures to regression test datasets.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The 5-Step Agent Regression Loop
- **How it works**: A continuous engineering workflow to test agent changes against production data before deployment.
- **Components**:
  - Observe: Trace every agent run in production
  - Evaluate: Score live traces with standardized evaluators
  - Change: Edit prompt, model, tool, skill, or policy
  - Test: Run regression experiments in CI/CD against evaluation gates
  - Improve: Ship what passes and feed new failures back into test datasets
- **When to use**: Whenever making modifications to LLM prompts, agent policies, tool definitions, or underlying models in production applications.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A security engineer added a one-line policy requiring the support agent to confirm before taking any action.
- **Illustrates**: Unintended side effects of localized prompt changes on multi-step workflows.
- **Lesson**: Action safety improved by 17% (+0.17), but task completion dropped by 17% (-0.17), resulting in a net-zero overall average improvement.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Pull real production traces including normal workflows, known failures, edge cases, and successful workflows into evaluation datasets.
  - Combine code-based evaluators for deterministic checks with LLM-as-a-judge evaluators for semantic metrics.
  - Integrate agent evaluation suites into GitHub Actions or CI/CD pipelines as merge gates.
- **Strategic**:
  - Treat production traces as the authoritative source of truth for agent behavior.
  - Shift from human manual triage to automated agent-driven self-correction and testing.
  - Ensure every production failure automatically updates and strengthens the regression test suite.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can agents autonomously propose and test prompt or policy fixes based on trace failures?
  - What is the optimal balance between LLM-as-a-judge evaluation cost and accuracy in CI pipelines?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- The diff tells you what changed, but the trace tells you what it actually did (conceptual)
- The best agents don't just learn from failures; they fix themselves (visionary)
## Notable Quotes

> "The logic only exists at runtime."
> "Every failure should become a test."
> "The best agents don't just learn from failures. They fix themselves."
## Compressed Summary
- Agent regressions manifest at runtime rather than compile time.
- Code diffs fail to capture behavioral changes in LLM agents.
- A 5-step regression loop leverages production traces, evaluators, baselines, and CI gates.
- LLM-as-a-judge converts subjective agent metrics into actionable numeric scores.
- Automating evaluation in CI/CD prevents shipping broken agent changes.

- **Core insight**: Agent observability must evolve from a debugging dashboard for humans into an automated regression loop where production failures continuously strengthen agent test suites.
